g.text: Identify the write amplification and remove it BEFORE choosing the engine
Moving two mutable fields out of the index cuts writes 4x - and it helps whichever engine you pick, which is why it comes first.
Every intuition from building a search engine points the wrong way here
web search
EMAIL SEARCH
corpus
the whole internet, shared by everyone
ONE user's mailbox, private to them
ranking
by RELEVANCE - the hard problem
by DATE. Users want the recent one.
read:write ratio
read-heavy: index once, query billions of times
WRITE-HEAVY: 40B writes/day, a few queries/user/week
index freshness
minutes to hours is fine
SECONDS - the mail you just received must be findable
result completeness
approximate is fine (top 10 of millions)
EXACT. 'I know that email exists' - missing it is a bug.
index size per query
enormous
TINY - one mailbox
Two of those rows change the design fundamentally. It is WRITE-HEAVY - nearly unique among search systems - because every
received email, every send and every metadata change is an index write: 40 billion index writes/day against maybe a few
hundred million queries. So the engine must be optimized for INGEST, not for query throughput.
And RESULTS MUST BE EXACT. Web search returning the best 10 of a million matches is a feature; email search failing to surface
a message the user knows exists is a bug, and the kind users notice and remember. So there is no room for the
approximate-recall techniques that make web-scale search affordable.
The one thing that makes it tractable: THE QUERY SCOPE IS ONE MAILBOX. A search never spans users, so the index partitions by
user_id and every query is single-partition over a small dataset. That property is doing all the work below.
The reduction that comes before the engine choice
INDEXED - immutable, safe to index once and never rewrite
subject, body (plain text extracted from HTML), from, to, cc,
attachment filenames, attachment text content, date
NOT INDEXED - mutable, lives only in the metadata store
is_read, folder_id, labels, is_starred
Lucene documents are IMMUTABLE, so marking an email read means writing a
tombstone and indexing a whole new document - reindexing the entire 50 KB body
to flip a boolean. A brutal amplification for the single most common metadata
change in the product, and the detail that matters most.
So: index only the immutable content, and keep mutable state in the metadata
store. A search becomes two steps - query the index for matching message_ids,
then filter and enrich from the metadata store - which converts 'reindex 50 KB
to flip a bit' into 'update one small row'.
before
40 BILLION index writes / day
after
10 billion - only genuinely new messages
A 4x cut, and metadata changes no longer touch the index at all. Doing this reduction well is most of the engineering - and it
works regardless of which engine you pick, so do it FIRST. Reaching for a custom store before doing it would have solved the
wrong problem expensively.
Then, and only then, the engine choice
Elasticsearch, sharded by user_id
POST /emails/_doc { user_id, message_id, subject, body, from,
to, attachment_names, date }
GET /emails/_search { query: { bool: {
filter: [ {term: {user_id: 12345}} ],
must: [ {match: {body: 'invoice'}} ] } },
sort: [ {date: 'desc'} ] }
Full-text search that works out of the box: stemming, tokenization for
many languages, phrase queries, fuzzy matching, faceting, and mature
operational tooling. Sharding by user_id makes routing trivial and
means queries never fan out.
Where it struggles is specifically the WRITE path. Each write is a
document insert into a segment, and Lucene periodically MERGES segments
- read-and-rewrite amplification competing with ingest for the same
disk. At sustained high write rates, merge pressure becomes the binding
constraint. It is also a second system to operate, with its own
cluster, replication, backups and failure modes, alongside a metadata
store that already holds the same data.
a custom LSM-based per-user inverted index
write path - append-only, sequential:
1. new email -> tokenize -> posting entries in a memtable
2. memtable full -> flush SEQUENTIALLY to an immutable
on-disk sorted file
3. background: merge small files into larger ones
read path: query the memtable + each on-disk level, merge
LSM's whole premise is that WRITES ARE SEQUENTIAL APPENDS AND READS PAY
THE COST - and sequential disk is ~244x faster than random, so an
ingest-dominated workload wants exactly this trade. Same structure as
Cassandra, RocksDB and BigTable, and the same structure the metadata
store already uses - so the index can live IN the metadata store,
keyed by user_id, eliminating a second system entirely. Tuned for one
mailbox, with no merge contention across users.
The costs are large and mostly human: you are building a search
engine. Tokenization, stemming, stop words, Unicode normalization, CJK
segmentation, phrase queries, ranking - each a well-understood problem
with a long tail of correctness bugs, and 80 languages means 80 tails.
Plus read amplification across levels (mitigated by a Bloom filter per
file, which is exactly why LSM stores ship with them), and none of
Elasticsearch's decade of production hardening.
START with Elasticsearch and the mutable-field reduction. SWITCH to a custom LSM index when merge pressure is MEASURABLY the binding constraint.
With the reduction done, Elasticsearch's remaining weakness is merge pressure at 10 billion writes/day - demanding but not
obviously infeasible, and mitigated by per-user sharding (merges stay local) and by tuning refresh intervals against the
seconds-freshness requirement. At Gmail's scale the crossover point arrives, which is why Gmail does not run Elasticsearch.
Below it, building a multilingual search engine to avoid operating a cluster is a bad trade - years of engineering to save a
cluster.
Seconds of freshness, without tightening the refresh interval
mail processing worker
-> INSERT the metadata row (SYNCHRONOUS - the mail exists now)
-> enqueue a search-index write (async, seconds behind)
Asynchronous indexing means a brief window where a message is in the inbox but
not in the index. Usually invisible - users read new mail from the inbox and
search it days later - and noticeable in exactly one case: searching for
something that arrived moments ago.
the hybrid query
index -> older matches
metadata -> scan the user's most recent N messages directly
union the two
Recent mail is a tiny set and already cached, since access is heavily
recency-skewed, so scanning it is cheap. This is the same
FILTER-THEN-VERIFY / index-plus-recent-scan shape that recurs across this
guide: the index handles the bulk, and a cheap exact pass handles the part the
index has not caught up with.
Strictly better than tightening the index refresh interval, which would
increase merge pressure to fix a problem affecting a narrow slice of queries.
Two details in what gets indexed that are bigger than they look
HTML must be reduced to plain text before indexing
Indexing raw HTML means matching on tag names and CSS class names, so a search for 'table' returns every email containing
one. Extraction also has to handle the tracking pixels, hidden preheader text and invisible white-on-white keyword stuffing
that marketing and spam email are full of - some of which is DELIBERATELY trying to pollute the index.
attachment content extraction is a large, separate problem
Searching inside PDFs and documents is genuinely valuable, and it means running parsers over UNTRUSTED attachments - an attack
surface, since document parsers are a historically rich source of memory-safety exploits. That work belongs in a sandboxed
worker, not in the indexing path, which is why it is an enhancement rather than a given.
